prompt: A program calls `purchases.cache()`. When is the copy filled?
hint: Is `cache()` an action?

choices.text: By the first action that computes `purchases`
choices.why: Right. `cache()` only marks the DataFrame.

choices.text: When the application ends
choices.why: That is when it is dropped.

choices.text: At once, before `cache()` returns
choices.why: That is SQL's `CACHE TABLE`, not `cache()`.

choices.text: At the second action on it
choices.why: The first action fills it; the second reads it.

prompt: With a cache, the first action's tasks worked 20.0 seconds in total, and without one 15.2. What was the extra work?
hint: What else did it do besides counting?

choices.text: It also built the cached copy
choices.why: Right. The first use pays for the copy.

choices.text: A cached DataFrame is read row by row
choices.why: The cache is columnar, and it was being filled, not read.

choices.text: The cache switched off adaptive execution for that query
choices.why: It changes nothing about adaptive execution.

choices.text: The cache moved all the data through the driver first
choices.why: Each executor caches its own partitions.

prompt: Without a cache each action costs 6 seconds. With one, the first costs 8 and each later one 1. From how many actions is the cache cheaper in total?
hint: Compare 6n with 8 + (n − 1).

prompt: Match each storage level to what happens to a partition that does not fit in memory.
hint: One of them keeps nothing.

pairs.right: It goes to the executor's local disk
It is recomputed every time it is needed
It goes to disk, on two executors

right_distractors: It is sent to the driver

prompt: At `MEMORY_ONLY`, three of 45 partitions did not fit. Why did counting again take 8.6 seconds instead of under two?
hint: Where did those three come from the second time?

choices.text: Spark wrote the missing three to disk first
choices.why: At `MEMORY_ONLY` nothing goes to disk.

choices.text: The second count cleared the whole cache and started it again
choices.why: 42 partitions stayed cached.

choices.text: They were read from the files again
choices.why: Right. A partition not kept is recomputed every time.

choices.text: Partitions in memory are slower than on disk
choices.why: Memory is the fast part.

prompt: Why did the cached clicks take less memory than their 396 MB of Parquet files?
hint: In what form does a DataFrame's cache keep rows?

choices.text: Part of the copy went to the executors' disks without being reported
choices.why: The page reported 0.0 MiB on disk.

choices.text: Spark caches them in its own compressed columnar form
choices.why: Right. Not as one object per row.

choices.text: The cache drops duplicate rows
choices.why: A cache never changes the rows.

choices.text: Only the columns that `count` needed were kept in the cache
choices.why: A cache holds every column of the DataFrame.

prompt: Which of these are good candidates for a cache? Choose all that apply.
hint: Used more than once, and expensive to make.

choices.text: The raw clicks, straight after the read, for one query
choices.why: One use, and Parquet's read is already cheap.

choices.text: The links read by every iteration of a loop
choices.why: Yes. That is section 04.

choices.text: A join's result that three reports read
choices.why: Yes. The join is saved twice.

choices.text: A DataFrame written to Parquet once and never read again
choices.why: One use: the cache only adds its cost.

prompt: A cache that was complete a minute ago now has missing partitions, and no error was raised. What most likely happened?
hint: Storage memory is shared with something.

choices.text: The Parquet files changed underneath
choices.why: Spark does not watch the files.

choices.text: Running tasks needed that memory for their work
choices.why: Right. They evicted the least recently used partitions first.

choices.text: The driver wrote them to the checkpoint directory
choices.why: Checkpoints only happen when asked for.

choices.text: The cache expires after sixty seconds
choices.why: A cache has no time limit.

prompt: In SQL, `CACHE ___ TABLE purchases AS SELECT ...` waits for the first query to fill the copy, as `cache()` does.
hint: The opposite of eager.

prompt: In `pagerank.py`, what stays on the cluster and what goes back to the driver each iteration?
hint: Which is millions of rows and which is 3,000 numbers?

choices.text: Both stay, and nothing returns until the end
choices.why: That is section 06's version, with a growing plan.

choices.text: Both come back to the driver every iteration
choices.why: The links never leave the cluster.

choices.text: The links stay; the ranks come back
choices.why: Right. Small state in the driver, large invariant data cached.

choices.text: The ranks stay; the links come back
choices.why: The links are far too many for the driver.

prompt: Put one iteration of `pagerank.py` in order.
hint: It starts in the driver and ends there.
items: Turn the ranks into a DataFrame
Join the links to the ranks by source book
Sum what each destination book receives
Collect the sums and damp them into new ranks

prompt: After an executor holding cached partitions dies, what does the next action do?
hint: The driver still knows how each partition was made.

choices.text: Fails, because cached data cannot be rebuilt
choices.why: Only a local checkpoint has nothing to rebuild from.

choices.text: Recomputes every partition, cached or not
choices.why: Only the missing ones: 14.6 s, not the first 37.6.

choices.text: Recomputes the missing ones from their lineage
choices.why: Right, and caches them again.

choices.text: Waits for the executor to come back with its memory
choices.why: A new executor starts empty.

prompt: To keep every cached partition on two executors, persist with the level `MEMORY_AND_DISK___`.
hint: A suffix of two characters.

prompt: The plan had 291 lines after five iterations and 576 after ten. How many lines did each iteration add?
hint: Five iterations between the two.

prompt: What does a very long lineage cost? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three places were named.

choices.text: More disk space in the checkpoint directory
choices.why: A lineage is a plan, not files.

choices.text: Planning time at every action
choices.why: Yes. The whole plan is analysed each time.

choices.text: Longer recomputation after a failure
choices.why: Yes. A lost partition may need every earlier step.

choices.text: A stack overflow in the driver, past some depth
choices.why: Yes, with an error that names no line of the program.

prompt: Why does Spark warn about a checkpoint directory on the local filesystem?
hint: Who writes it and who reads it back?

choices.text: Checkpoints must be encrypted
choices.why: Nothing here is about encryption.

choices.text: Local disks are too slow for checkpoints
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Other machines' executors could not read it back
choices.why: Right. It belongs on HDFS or an object store.

choices.text: A local directory fills up faster than one in HDFS would
choices.why: Space is not the reason.

prompt: Match each call to what is true of it.
hint: Only one survives a lost executor.

pairs.right: Writes to shared storage and survives a lost executor
Cuts the plan, and a lost executor fails the job
Keeps the plan, and rebuilds what is lost

right_distractors: Writes the plan itself to a file

prompt: Why is caching the raw clicks straight after `read.parquet` usually a poor trade?
hint: What would the cache save?

choices.text: A cached DataFrame cannot be filtered
choices.why: It can, like any other.

choices.text: The cache would be written to the Parquet files
choices.why: A cache lives in the executors.

choices.text: It saves only a read that Parquet already makes cheap
choices.why: Right, and holds every column to do it.

choices.text: Spark refuses to cache a table read from files
choices.why: This lesson cached exactly that.

prompt: Match each symptom to the change it calls for.
hint: Read what each one says about memory, time or plan.

pairs.left: Every iteration of a loop rereads the same input from files
pairs.right: Cache the input before the loop

pairs.left: Each iteration takes longer, though the work per iteration is the same
A sort spills since the program started caching everything
pairs.right: Unpersist what is no longer used

prompt: A cached result took an hour to compute, is read twenty times, and losing it to a dead executor would delay a report. Which level fits?
hint: What does a second copy buy?

choices.text: `MEMORY_ONLY`
choices.why: A partition that does not fit is recomputed every read.

choices.text: `localCheckpoint()`
choices.why: A lost executor would fail the job outright.

choices.text: `MEMORY_AND_DISK_2`
choices.why: Right. A lost executor costs a lookup, not an hour.

choices.text: `DISK_ONLY`
choices.why: One copy, so a lost executor still costs the hour.
